To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
we have developed a simple approach to predict the impact of temperature variations on data retention in floating gate EEPROM memories.
the temperature activation energy for SILC generation is about 0.4 eV and that AC generation and annealing kinetics are not affected by temperature.
we have shown the impact of the AC generation, the annealing kinetics and the temperature activation on the SILC evolution in a floating gate structure with a 6.8 nm oxide tunneling oxide.
In summary, our research is concerned with
a detailed study of SILC and its impact on EEPROM data retention in order to develop an analytical approach to predict the evolution of SILC during retention.
the development of a model for predicting the impact on data retention of the temperature and the stress time.
a detailed study of the SILC behavior of a floating gate structure in a wide range of temperatures (25 °C to 125 °C), and with the development of an accurate model to describe the SILC kinetics.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
SILC evolution during data retention can be described by an Arrhenius law.
SILC in EEPROM memories can be described as a function of temperature and time, and the activation energy can be determined for a given stress voltage.
the SILC evolution during the retention phases can be well described by an exponential function of the oxide floating gate potential and the temperature.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

we have demonstrated the possibility to obtain a good correlation between experimental and theoretical results for a wide range of temperature (25 °C–200 °C) and for a large range of retention time (10 s–10 h).

the stress induced leakage current is the result of the interaction of the following three phenomena: the generation of interface traps, the creation of oxide traps, the increase of oxide defects density.
the SILC evolution can be well described by a simple model which is based on the generation of interface states and the annealing kinetics of the oxide traps.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the SILC activation energy is not constant but varies with temperature and oxide potential.
the SILC evolution can be predicted by a single parameter which depends on the oxide thickness, the temperature and the oxide electric field.
the activation energy is not constant during stress, but rather increases with stress time.
